title: A Smile for the Room
premise: Silas Winterbourne returns to the family house to bury her twin brother, only to find that everyone in town—including her mother—insists it was Silas who died and 'the other one' who came home. Waiting on the porch is Wren, the imaginary friend she invented at six, unchanged by twenty years, who claims Silas was never imaginary at all but a changeling swapped at the well. As the household's rituals tighten around her—the nightly song, the counting of chairs, the well that refills on the equinox—Silas must decide whether to keep denying what she is or learn the song's last verse, which can either seal her back beneath the water or finally make her real. In the end she sings the verse wrong on purpose, breaking the bargain for every changeling in the valley, and chooses the imperfect family of survivors over the perfect one that made her.
about_author: Emrys Reyes is the pen name of a former hospice night nurse from coastal Maine who writes horror about the tenderness that survives grief. Their short fiction has appeared in several small-press anthologies, and this is their first novel.

chapters.title: The Wrong Grave
chapters.summary: Third-person limited, Silas's POV. Silas arrives for the funeral and hears her own name read over the casket; her mother greets her as a stranger and mourns 'Silas' as the dead twin. The emotional beat is disorientation sharpening into dread as Silas realizes denial will not be enough to get through the week.

chapters.title: Wren on the Porch
chapters.summary: Silas's POV. At dusk she finds Wren—her childhood imaginary friend, ageless, patient—waiting with tea and an apology for taking so long. Wren speaks in half-truths about the well and the song. The beat is uncanny comfort: the first person to treat Silas as real is the least real thing on the property.

chapters.title: Household Arithmetic
chapters.summary: Alternating POV with mother Odile. The house enforces its rituals: seven chairs for six people, salt lines renewed at midnight, a lullaby sung before bed that no one will finish. Odile's chapters reveal she has buried a child before. The beat is claustrophobic domesticity where love and captivity are indistinguishable.

chapters.title: What the Well Remembers
chapters.summary: Wren's POV, the first time we leave Silas's head. Wren recalls the original bargain: a child given to the well each generation, a changeling left in its place, and a song whose last verse returns the taken one home. Wren was the previous payment. The beat is guilt—Wren loves Silas and has been complicit all along.

chapters.title: The Other One
chapters.summary: Silas's POV. She finds her brother's room untouched and, inside it, evidence he spent years investigating the family: photographs of children who 'came back wrong,' a journal naming Silas as the swap. The beat is betrayal curdling into a terrible relief—if she was never their daughter, her loneliness had a reason.

chapters.title: Neighbors Who Count
chapters.summary: Ensemble POV through the wake. Townsfolk arrive with casseroles and scrutiny, testing Silas with childhood riddles she cannot answer, marking her hands for webbing between the fingers. One old woman, Maren, quietly slips her a warning: the well refills at the equinox, three days away. The beat is exposure—the mask slipping in public.

chapters.title: Last Verse, First Attempt
chapters.summary: Dual POV, Silas and Wren. Wren teaches Silas the song in the cellar, but the final verse requires singing along with something answering from below—and when Silas tries, her voice harmonizes without her consent, and the well water rises a foot overnight. The beat is temptation: the song offers belonging, and part of her wants it.

chapters.title: Odile's Confession
chapters.summary: Odile's POV. On the eve of the equinox, Odile admits she has known since the cradle—that she chose to raise the changeling because the child the well returned was cold in a way she could not love. Her grief for 'Silas' was always grief for the daughter she refused. The beat is devastating honesty: duty won, and it cost them both.

chapters.title: Equinox
chapters.summary: Silas's POV, climax. The family drags her to the well to sing her home; Wren breaks ranks to stand beside her; the water rises and calls with her brother's stolen voice. Silas sings the last verse deliberately wrong—a broken cadence Wren taught her as a child—and the well cracks, spilling out every changeling ever traded. The beat is defiance becoming liberation.

chapters.title: A Smile for the Room
chapters.summary: Silas's POV, resolution. The house settles into ordinary disrepair; Odile, stripped of ritual, awkwardly learns to mother the daughter she actually has; Wren, now mortal and aging, moves into the brother's room. At the funeral they finally hold, Silas smiles—not performed, not required—for the small room of misfits who stayed. The beat is quiet, earned belonging.
